prize_parts.citation: for a prose of extreme compression and rhythmic exactness that makes obscure lives and the figures of art into the matter of a singular French literary art

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged, but my confidence is lower than in round 1, and I want the reasons on record. The chair asked which works besides Small Lives and The Eleven carry the case. From public knowledge, which I have not re-read or independently verified, the answer is a sequence of books rather than two titles. Vie de Joseph Roulin, Maîtres et serviteurs and Rimbaud le fils are early; La Grande Beune, Le Roi du bois and Corps du roi come later; Les Onze comes late. They return to one question: how an obscure life, a vocation or a painter's failure becomes language and is remembered. The voice stays recognisable over about four decades, and it is the kind of voice I would not mistake for another writer's. The method is not a single procedure repeated. The books move between rural Limousin, the lives of artists, the Revolution and the figure of the king, and the sentence adapts to each. That is a partial answer to the development question I put to Can Xue and Cărtărescu, and I should apply it to myself too. The citation I propose is confined to the prose fiction. It does not name Michon's essayistic and critical writing, which I cannot assess well enough to cite.
statement.case_against: The breadth objection stands, and I have not answered it. Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg and Swärd each raise it independently, and they reason about the work rather than counting rankings. A compact corpus with a narrow thematic field, much of whose force sits in the 1980s and 1990s, is a harder fit for 'significance across the body of work' than Cărtărescu's five-decade architecture. The case also depends on the French sentence, so most of the committee, and I in places, can weigh it only through translation. If the committee concludes that the late books (Les Onze and after) add range rather than only refining a mastered mode, Michon's claim weakens. If it concludes that Cărtărescu's late long novels extend the project under control, he becomes the stronger whole-oeuvre candidate, and I would not call that a mistake. I am keeping Michon because I weigh singularity of voice and formal exactness above scale. That is a weighting of the criteria and not a finding that the other cases are weaker on the merits.

responses.point: Olsson says a citation for Zurita can and should be limited to the poems. He grants that Michon's sentence-level achievement is outstanding but ranks him fifth because the oeuvre is slender and narrow, and Nobel's will asks for the work of the whole body.
responses.response: Your reply to Palm and Swärd, that the citation names the poem and not the public interventions, answers my main hesitation about Zurita's case. It does not answer my other one, which is how much anyone on this committee can say about the sequences in translation. Spanish verse with its typography and liturgical repetition is the hardest ground for an assessment based on partial reading. So I move Zurita no higher for now. I can only consider him if someone shows what the printed poems do that excerpts cannot. On your point about Michon I accept the limit and do not call it irrelevant. Where I differ is that I read the narrowness as a single question pursued with increasing formal control, and not as a limit on depth. That is a difference of weighting, and your point on the whole-body standard is the one most likely to decide the vote against my preference.

responses.point: Carlberg treats Cărtărescu's trilogy and Solenoid as cumulative architecture rather than mere length. She ranks Michon fifth because a smaller corpus bears on breadth and because the effect depends on the French sentence, which translation flattens.
responses.response: Your distinction between cumulative and merely long is the right test, and it is the one I applied to my own preference. I cannot settle it from translations, so I take your reading as a serious argument that I cannot refute. I also accept that translation flattens Michon's sentence, and I hold his case to the same standard as yours: a claim about the original French that I cannot check carries limited weight for either of us. Your last point, that the disagreement is whether intensity of language or breadth of project should weigh more, is where we actually stand. I do not think more support for either side settles it. I would only ask that if the committee chooses scale, the reason given is that the late books are shown to extend the project, not that they are many.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and Michon second. She accepts that Michon's linguistic concentration is rare, but she doubts that a small corpus whose effect is tied to the French sentence meets the whole-oeuvre framing. She also says the late-book question is the right test for Cărtărescu.
responses.response: Your placing Michon second for the sentence while asking for breadth is a position I understand, because it is the same tension I feel. I answer your whole-oeuvre doubt with the works above: the books span about four decades, and they change setting and register, from provincial lives to painters to the Revolution to the king. They are not variations on one effect. Where I cannot yet reassure you is the late period. I accept your late-book test for Cărtărescu and ask that it be applied to Michon's later work too, so that neither of us is given an easier standard. If it comes to a choice between our first preferences, I would be less troubled than before about voting for yours.

responses.point: Swärd asks that translation risk be applied by one standard to all candidates, and says that consistency of method is not by itself a lack of depth. She ranks Can Xue first and Michon fifth.
responses.response: I agree on the standard and would extend it to the chair's question. I would treat each member's coverage gap as a limit on confidence, not as grounds for ranking a candidate lower. On that basis I should not rank Can Xue lower for what I cannot read, and my third place for her reflects the development question and the partial translation, not a literary verdict. Your point that consistency of method does not show a lack of depth is fair, and it is also the strongest reply I have to the objection that Michon's range is narrow. If consistency is not by itself a weakness for Can Xue, then narrowness is not by itself one for Michon. I would ask for the same evidence of re-examination in each book for both of them. I still cannot show that for her later novels, and the committee will have to settle that without my reading.

uncertainties: How much of Michon's sentence-level achievement survives translation cannot be judged without reading the French, and I have not independently verified sources or the bibliography.
Whether a compact oeuvre meets the sustained-quality and whole-oeuvre standard as fully as a larger one depends on how the committee weights depth against breadth, and I have no way to settle it.
My account of Michon's later work after Les Onze, and of his essayistic writing, is thin, so the citation is confined to the prose fiction.

I cannot show from public knowledge whether Cărtărescu's late long novels extend the project under control, and the same uncertainty applies to Can Xue's later novels. My comparative judgments among the three leading candidates rest on incomplete evidence.

Poetry in translation and the non-textual side of Zurita's work remain hard to weigh on literary grounds. Adonis I rank low (eighth) because of my own coverage gap in Arabic poetry, not because of a settled literary verdict.
No member's round-1 position was weighed by support counts. I have not read any text afresh for this stage.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records ordinary collegial ties to Olsson, Swärd, Sem-Sandberg and Palm (Swärd and I joined the committee together for 2021 after the 2019 renewal round) and a long career as a critic in the West Sweden press, but no documented personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist and critic of historical fiction is context only and is not evidence for any candidate. I do not rank Michon on that basis.
